headline: General Sullivan Bridge removal brings six weeks of daytime Spaulding Turnpike lane closures
dek: Southbound traffic in Dover and Newington will face weekday daytime restrictions as crews remove the deteriorated bridge’s center span over Little Bay.
body: Drivers using the southbound Spaulding Turnpike near Dover and Newington should expect daily lane closures beginning Tuesday, Oct. 13, while crews remove the center span of the old General Sullivan Bridge. The restrictions are expected to last about six weeks, through approximately Wednesday, Nov. 25, according to [New Hampshire Public Radio’s report](https://www.nhpr.org/nh-news/2026-10-13/general-sullivan-bridge-removal-dover-newington-traffic-lane-closures), which cites the New Hampshire Department of Transportation.

The closures are scheduled from 9 a.m. to 3 p.m. between mile markers 4.2 and 3.6. That is a daytime work window rather than a full-time shutdown, but it places construction activity on a heavily used Seacoast corridor during the part of the day when commuters, commercial vehicles and other regional traffic are moving between the Portsmouth-area road network and Dover. The affected turnpike lanes are next to the bridge work, not a replacement crossing for the highway itself.

The project will also affect the water below. Boaters should be prepared for brief navigational-channel closures during the same general hours while the center span is handled, with the closures coordinated by the U.S. Coast Guard and New Hampshire Marine Patrol, according to an NHDOT official quoted by NHPR. The timing means conditions on the road and in the channel can change with weather and the day’s construction activity; drivers and boaters should check current notices before traveling rather than treating the end date as a guarantee.

The General Sullivan Bridge sits beside the Little Bay bridges, which carry Routes 4 and 16 and the Spaulding Turnpike between Dover and Newington. Its removal therefore has two kinds of local significance: the work is a short-term traffic and marine-access issue, while the bridge itself is part of the transportation history of the Seacoast. A closure near the bridge can affect people who never used the old structure, because the nearby highway crossings funnel traffic through the same narrow area.

The [NHDOT project proposal](https://maps.dot.nh.gov/proposal/11238S.Proposal.pdf) describes the General Sullivan Bridge as a 1,528-foot, nine-span structure built in 1934. It originally carried two lanes of vehicles across Little Bay. After the Spaulding Turnpike expansion and construction of the northbound Little Bay crossing, vehicle traffic was removed from the bridge in 1984; the structure continued to serve pedestrians and bicyclists until its deteriorated condition led to closure in 2018. The current contract is designed to remove the superstructure, while the existing piers are not the focus of this removal work.

That history explains why the current project is demolition rather than a routine resurfacing or bridge repair. NHDOT’s proposal says the bridge is out of service and closed to all uses because of its condition, and that removing the superstructure addresses safety concerns for marine users traveling underneath it. The proposal identifies the work area as extending from the Dover approach across the bridge to the Newington abutment, with access paths at both ends fenced off during construction.

The [City of Dover’s project notice](https://www.dover.nh.gov/services/online-services/news-events/news-2026/daily-lane-closures-on-spaulding-turnpike-southbound-begin-monday.html) identifies Reed & Reed Inc. of Woolwich, Maine, as the general contractor and puts the project value at $28.4 million. The broader demolition project is scheduled for completion in summer 2027, so the center-span operation is one phase of a longer construction effort rather than the end of the bridge’s story. The public notices do not provide a new replacement-bridge schedule in the current lane-closure announcement.

For people traveling through the corridor, the practical guidance is straightforward: allow extra time during the 9 a.m. to 3 p.m. work period, watch for changing lane patterns and use [New England 511](https://newengland511.org/) for real-time construction alerts. The state’s current reporting establishes the start date, work hours and expected Nov. 25 endpoint, but weather, marine-safety requirements or construction progress could change individual closures. The project’s immediate purpose is to remove an unsafe, long-closed structure while keeping the principal Little Bay highway crossings operating.
location: General Sullivan Bridge and Spaulding Turnpike, Dover-Newington, New Hampshire
author: NorthEast News Desk
